To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
We show that a modified monocular visual SLAM system provides improved pose estimation for the localisation of a transportation asset management survey vehicle.

We show that the use of DNNs to estimate the pose of a highway surveying vehicle, from images captured using a monocular camera, improves upon the accuracy and reliability of the estimation provided by a standard vSLAM approach.

we have modified the ORB-SLAM2 vSLAM system to overcome the two main problems with using vSLAM on highway imagery, namely the presence of other cars and the lack of parallax on straight segments of highway.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the localisation of a surveying vehicle using vSLAM and DNNs, and the application of this work to TAM.
the development of vSLAM systems for highway surveying, which can be applied to TAM, and other autonomous vehicles.
how vSLAM systems can be applied to the localisation of vehicles, and how DNNs can be used to improve the accuracy of such systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed method is capable of providing a more accurate estimate of the vehicle’s location, and that this estimate can be improved further by using a more powerful deep learning network.
the proposed method is a viable solution to the problem of visual localisation in highway scenes.
the use of a monocular vSLM system, combined with DNNs, is an effective means of localising the pose of a surveying vehicle on a highway.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed an augmented vSLAM method for highway asset survey, which is capable of estimating the pose (position + orientation) of the camera.
we have developed a vSLAM system that can estimate the pose of a vehicle surveyor on highways, and that this is a step forward in the application of vSLAM systems in TAM and autonomous vehicles.
the use of a DNN to detect the road surface, and a DNN to segment out other vehicles in the visual scene can significantly improve the performance of a vSLAM system when applied to highway imagery.
The main takeaway from our work is that

vSLAM systems are capable of estimating the pose of a survey vehicle with sufficient accuracy for TAM purposes, even when there are straight sections of highway, and even when there is other vehicle movement in the visual field.
vSLAM systems can be improved with DNNs, and that the resulting system can provide accurate pose estimates in a challenging environment.
DNNs can be used to improve the estimation of pose in a vSLAM system.
